canonicalExplanation.summary: An **array** stores items side by side in memory, so the computer can jump straight to position i: **reading or writing `a[i]` is O(1)**. But the items are packed with no gaps, so **inserting or deleting in the middle** means **shifting** every item after that spot, which is O(n) in the worst case. Adding or removing **at the end** is O(1) (amortised, for growable arrays like Python lists, C++ `vector` or Java `ArrayList`). Searching an unsorted array for a value is O(n).

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A class register keeps learner names in an array in joining order. When a late joiner must go in at position 2 of 5, the code writes `a[2] = name` and one learner vanishes from the register. Inserting at index two of five values shifts three existing values before writing the new one. In this lesson you'll implement and test core array operations and explain their complexity.

```predict
{"question": "`a = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]`. To insert 99 at index 2 keeping every value, how many existing values move?", "options": ["0: just write a[2] = 99", "3: 30, 40 and 50 each shift one place right"], "answer": 1, "why": "Writing a[2] overwrites 30. Insertion shifts the suffix right first."}
```

sections.heading: The distinction: jump to a slot vs shift a suffix
sections.body:
```python
def insert_at(a, index, value):
    # Precondition: 0 <= index <= len(a).
    a.append(None)                        # make room at the end.
    for k in range(len(a) - 1, index, -1):   # shift right, back to front.
        a[k] = a[k - 1]
    a[index] = value

def delete_at(a, index):
    # Precondition: 0 <= index < len(a).
    removed = a[index]
    for k in range(index, len(a) - 1):    # shift left, front to back.
        a[k] = a[k + 1]
    a.pop()                               # drop the duplicate last slot.
    return removed

register = ["Asha", "Ben", "Chen", "Dev", "Ema"]
insert_at(register, 2, "Farah")         # Chen, Dev, Ema shift right.
```

| Operation | Cost |
|---|---|
| read or write a[i]. | O(1). |
| append / pop at end. | O(1) amortised. |
| insert or delete at i. | O(n - i) shifts, O(n) worst. |
| find a value (unsorted). | O(n). |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why shift from the back when inserting?", "answer": "Shifting front to back would copy a[2] into a[3], then that same value into a[4], and so on, overwriting everything with one value."}
```

examples.title: Squeezing a value into the middle
examples.situation: Inserting at index two of five values shifts three existing values before writing the new one.
walkthrough: **Make room:** append a placeholder so the array has six slots.
**Shift three existing values:** Ema, Dev, then Chen move one place right, working from the back.
**Write and test:** Farah goes into index 2; tests will check inserting at 0, at 2 and at the end.
examples.result: The register holds all six learners in the right order, and nobody is overwritten.

examples.title: The delete that left a copy
examples.situation: A delete function shifts values left but forgets to shrink the array, so [1, 2, 3] minus index 0 becomes [2, 3, 3].
walkthrough: After shifting, the last slot still holds the old last value.
The array must shrink by one (pop in Python, size-- in C, remove in Java lists).
examples.result: Deleting leaves exactly n - 1 values with no duplicate at the end.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Every array operation is constant time because indexing is constant time.
misconceptions.correction: Only reading or writing a known index is O(1). Inserting or deleting away from the end shifts the following items, which costs time proportional to how many move: O(n) in the worst case.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "Squeezing a value into the middle", how many values moved?

analogy.example: An array is like **a row of numbered theatre seats**. Finding seat 7 is instant. But if someone must sit in seat 3 and everyone must stay in order, the people in seats 3, 4 and 5 each shuffle one seat right, starting from the end of the row.
usefulFor: shift from the back when inserting
limitations: Real rows have fixed length; dynamic arrays grow by moving to a bigger row.
Adding someone at the empty end seat needs no shuffling.

steps.explanation: Appending a placeholder gives one free slot at the end.
Inserting at index two of five values shifts three existing values.
The new value is written only after the shift.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing an array insertion. Step 1, Room: length is 6; a[5] is None. Appending a placeholder gives one free slot at the end. Step 2, Shift: moves is Ema→5, Dev→4, Chen→3. Inserting at index two of five values shifts three existing values. Step 3, Write: a is [Asha, Ben, Farah, Chen, Dev, Ema]. The new value is written only after the shift.

farTransfer.prompt: Build a fixed-capacity array class with get, set, insert_at, delete_at and len, raising errors for out-of-range indexes and a full array. Test every edge position and state each operation's complexity.

remediation.explanation: For each operation ask: **Do I know the index and just read or write it? (O(1)) Or do items after it have to move? (O(n))** Then test positions 0, middle and end.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The delete that left a copy".

recap.summary: To implement and test core array operations, remember indexing reads or writes in O(1), appending at the end is O(1) amortised, and inserting or deleting in the middle shifts the suffix in O(n). Shift from the back when inserting, shrink after deleting, and test the first, middle and last positions.
retrievalPrompts: Why is inserting in the middle O(n)?
Which direction do you shift when inserting?
